titulo: Why does it cool off suddenly after a storm?
destinatario: se lo manda alguien a su amigo que sale al patio apenas para la lluvia y dice 'finally, it cooled off'
fuentes: National Weather Service (NWS), Binghamton: 'Weather in Action: Downburst' (air cooled by evaporating raindrops sinks and spreads out in all directions, like a glass of water spilled on pavement)
NWS glossary: outflow boundary (similar in effect to a cold front, usually a drop in temperature)
NWS pages on heat bursts (rare cases where the sinking air arrives hot)

frases.texto: The storm ends and, all of a sudden, it's cooler. Where did that chill come from?
It didn't come from anywhere strange. The rain brought it.
frases.estilo: Dry and punchy, with a half smile.

frases.texto: Inside the cloud, raindrops evaporate, and evaporating pulls heat out of the air.
That cooled air is heavier than the air around it, so it sinks toward the ground.
The National Weather Service compares it to a glass of water spilled on pavement: when it hits the ground, it spreads out in every direction.
So it's, more or less, a cold front in miniature.
frases.estilo: Dry and punchy, with a half smile.

frases.texto: Heads up: not always. Every once in a while, the air coming down arrives hot.
Send this to the friend who steps outside and says, finally, it cooled off.
